sections.heading: Overshoot with RHPZ undershoot
sections.text: Boost overshoot under load step shows a characteristic initial dip (non-minimum-phase undershoot) before the output recovers. This is caused by the RHPZ. Fix: reduce voltage-loop crossover below RHPZ/4, increase inner current-loop bandwidth, or add input voltage feedforward.

sections.heading: Slow settling from RHPZ limit
sections.text: Slow settling on a boost usually means the voltage-loop bandwidth is below the RHPZ limit but gains are still too conservative. Check if the RHPZ frequency is lower than expected — this happens at light load (high R_load) or near-maximum duty cycle. Consider load-current feedforward.

sections.heading: Excess ripple from capacitor sizing
sections.text: Boost output ripple is dominated by the capacitor ESR and the charging/discharging current during switch on-time. At high duty cycle, the diode conducts for a short fraction of the period, so the capacitor must supply the load for most of the cycle. Verify C and ESR before changing gains.

sections.heading: Efficiency from conduction losses
sections.text: Boost efficiency is primarily a function of conduction losses (which increase with duty cycle) and diode forward voltage. From the control side: verify the operating point is not in deep DCM at light load. Consider synchronous rectification or interleaving.

sections.heading: RHPZ architecture limit
sections.text: If boost fails across multiple iterations with current-mode control and the RHPZ frequency is below the required bandwidth, the topology cannot meet the transient spec. Consider interleaved boost (reduces effective RHPZ), buck-boost, or a different topology family.
